1.33.m: Bhīṣma said: / How indeed was Rāma instructed here by Mārkaṇḍeya? / How did the meeting take place, at what time, and when, O sage?
Whose son was Mārkaṇḍeya of great austerities, and how was he born? / Tell me the origin of his name as it truly happened, O great sage.
Pulastya said: / Now I shall tell you the origin of Mārkaṇḍeya once more. / Formerly, in a past cosmic age, there was a renowned sage named Mṛkaṇḍu.
The son of Bhṛgu, highly fortunate, practiced austerities together with his wife. / A son was then born to him while living in the forest.
When he became five years old, a child endowed with excellent virtues, / he was seen wandering in his courtyard by a wise man.
Having stood for a very long time, he perceived what was to happen. / He was indeed asked by his father: 'How long is the lifespan of my son?'
'Count and declare his years, whether they be few or many.' / Thus addressed by Mṛkaṇḍu, that wise man spoke these words:
'The lifespan of your son ordained by the Creator is six months, O best of sages; / you must not grieve; this which is stated is true.'
Hearing that statement spoken by the wise man, O Bhīṣma, / the father then performed the sacred thread ceremony for the child.
And the father said to the son: 'Pay your respects to the sages.' / Thus addressed by his father, he was delighted in offering salutation.
He knew no distinction of classes, saluting everyone of all classes. / Five months and twenty-five days passed by.
Then seven sages came along that path; / they were seen by that child, and all of them were saluted.
'May you be long-lived,' said they to that child carrying a staff and wearing a girdle. / Having spoken thus, they again saw that the child's life was exhausted.
Knowing that his lifespan was five days, they were frightened, O king; / taking that child, they went into the presence of Brahmā.
Presenting him, O king, they bowed down before the Grandfather. / He was announced by them, and Brahmā was saluted by him.
The boy was told, 'Be long-lived,' by Brahmā in the presence of the sages; / then those sages were delighted, having heard the word from the Grandfather.
Seeing the sages, the Grandfather spoke, filled with wonder: / 'For what purpose have you come? Announce who this boy is.'
Then, O king, those sages reported everything to him: / 'He is the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, whose lifespan is exhausted; endow the boy with life.'
'Knowing he was short-lived, the sage bound this girdle on him, / gave him the sacred thread and a staff, and instructed him:'
"Whomever you see, child, wandering as a person upon the surface of the earth, / to him respect must be offered": thus spoke his father to him.
'Given to saluting, he was seen roaming on the earth / in the course of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, by the decree of fate, O Grandfather.'
"May you have a long life, my son!"—so was that boy addressed there: / "How might our words come true together with you?
Thus addressed by them then, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [said]: / 'This earth is established on truthful words, free from fear on every side.'
Brahmā said: / 'The child Mārkaṇḍeya will be equal to me in lifespan; / at the beginning and at the end of a cosmic age, he shall be considered the best of sages.'
Thus those sages, having accomplished it from the Grandfather in the world of Brahmā, / sent the boy back again to the surface of the earth.
The Brahmins departed on their pilgrimage; Mārkaṇḍeya went to his own home; / when they had departed, he then spoke to his father:
'I was taken to the world of Brahmā by sages who proclaim the Absolute; / I was granted long life, given boons, and dismissed.'
'This and another boon have been granted to me; the cause of your anxiety is gone: / at the beginning and at the end of a cosmic age, I shall exist continuously thereafter.'
'By the grace of Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, O father, / I shall go to Puṣkara, determined to practice austerities.'
'There I shall worship the Grandfather, the lord of the gods, / who grants all desires and slays all enemies,'
'the god who gives all happiness, the refuge of Indra and the others; / I shall propitiate Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds.'
Hearing the words of Mārkaṇḍeya, Mṛkaṇḍu, the best of sages, / felt the highest joy, sighing with relief for a moment.
Maintaining resolve with a delighted mind, he spoke these words: / 'Today my birth is fruitful, and my life is well-lived,'
'since the Grandfather, the creator of all the worlds, was seen. / Through you, a son who sustains the lineage, I possess an heir.'
'Go, see the Grandfather, the lord of the gods residing at Puṣkara; / when that lord of the universe is seen, old age and death are no more,'
'men obtain joys, sovereignty, and imperishable austerity. / There are three white peaks and three waterfalls,'
'and likewise three Puṣkaras; we do not know the reason for it: / the younger, the middle, and the third, Senior Puṣkara.'
'There are summits bearing names and auspicious streams; / the three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—are ever present there.'
'At the Puṣkaras, O great king, there is nothing holier on earth; / its dust-free, pure water is renowned across the three worlds.'
'The fortunate behold Puṣkara as the path to the world of Brahmā. / He who tends the sacred fire for fully a hundred years,'
'or dwells at Puṣkara for a single full moon day of Kārttika—these are equal; / that which could not be done by me, nor accomplished by action,'
'that all-destroying death has effortlessly been conquered by you, son; / there you have seen that lord of the gods, Brahmā, grandfather of the worlds.'
No other mortal like you will ever exist upon the surface of the earth, / by whom, with an existence of merely five years, I indeed have been pleased.
By my boon you will become the standard of comparison / for long-lived ones, there is no doubt; such is my blessing.
Speaking thus, they all said, "Go to whatever worlds you desire!" / And by the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, who had thus obtained their grace,
a hermitage was established by him, called the Mārkaṇḍa Hermitage. / Having bathed there and become pure, one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.
Cleansed of all sins in soul, a person becomes long-lived. / Pulastya said: / So I shall relate to you another ancient legendary history,
how indeed the sacred ford Puṣkara was constructed by Rāma. / Formerly, Rāma, [departing] from Citrakūṭa with the princess of Mithilā and Lakṣmaṇa,
arrived at the hermitage of Atri and inquired of that best of sages. / Rāma said: / "Which are the holy fords, or what is the sacred place, O great sage,
having gone to which a man never suffers separation from his kinsmen, / O yogin, O blessed one? Tell me that, O you of virtuous vows!
By this dwelling in the forest, and by the death of the king, / and by separation from Bharata, indeed I am tormented by these three."
Hearing that speech spoken by Rāghava, the bull among brāhmaṇas then, / having meditated for a very long time, spoke this word:
Atri said: / "Well asked by you, O hero, increaser of the Raghu lineage! / There is a sacred ford made by my father, renowned by the name of Puṣkara.
Two mountains are famous: the Maryādā and Yajña mountains. / Between the two lies a triad of pools: the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
Having gone to them, satisfy Daśaratha with an offering of rice-balls! / It is the best ford among fords, and the highest among sacred places.
There is the step-well Aviyogā ('Non-separation') and Surasā, O bearer of the Raghu race, / as well as another, the Saubhāgya well ('Well of Good Fortune'), with sweet water, O joy of the Raghus.
By offering rice-balls in them, the ancestors attain liberation / until the time of the dissolution of the elements: this the grandfather [Brahmā] proclaimed.
Go there, O Rāghava, and let your return [home] be accomplished!" / Saying "So be it," Rāma directed his mind toward departure.
Crossing the Ṛkṣavant mountain and the city of Vidiśā, / and having crossed the Carmaṇvatī, he reached the Yajña mountain.
Having passed beyond it swiftly, he stayed at the middle Puṣkara. / He gratified his ancestors and all the gods with waters.
At the conclusion of the bath, the wise Rāma saw / the bull among sages, Mārkaṇḍa, arriving there accompanied by disciples.
Having gone before him and bowed down with reverence, / he asked: "In which direction is the well that bestows non-separation, O lord?
I am the son of Daśaratha, remembered by people by the name of Rāma. / I have arrived by the command of Atri to behold that step-well of good fortune.
Let the venerable lord tell me that place and the two wells." / Addressed thus by Rāma, Mārkaṇḍa replied:
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / "Well done, Rāghava, good fortune to you! A virtuous deed has been done by you, / since on the occasion of pilgrimage to holy fords you have arrived here now.
Come, come, behold that step-well that grants non-separation! / And non-separation from all indeed arises at this well,
in the next world and in this one, whether one is living or dead." / Hearing this speech of the lord of sages, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāma, then remembered King Daśaratha, O king, / and Bharata along with Śatrughna, his other brothers, and the citizens.
While he was contemplating in this manner, the evening twilight arrived. / Having observed the evening twilight along with the sages, Rāghava
slept that night there, accompanied by his brother and wife. / At the end of the night, as the dream drew to a close, the joy of the Raghus [saw]:
He was dwelling in Ayodhyā along with his father, mother, and others; / during the marriage festivities, with many relatives,
he sat with his wife, surrounded by sages. / Lakṣmaṇa too saw in the very same way, and so did Sītā.
In the morning, all of that was reported to the sages. / And by the ṛṣis he was told: "So it is; this is true, O best of the Raghus.
Upon seeing one who has died, a śrāddha is remembered as obligatory to be performed. / The ancestors, desiring prosperity and craving food,
grant a vision in a dream to one endowed with devotion, O Rāghava. / And your non-separation from your brother, father, and Bharata
will surely happen, O Rāghava, after fourteen years. / Therefore perform the śrāddha of King Daśaratha, O hero!
And all these ṛṣis are devoted to you and ready: / I, and Jamadagni, and Bhāradvāja, and Lomaśa,
Devarāta, and Śamīka—these six are indeed the best of twice-borns. / Bring forth the materials for your śrāddha, O mighty-armed one:
chiefly ingudī oil-cake, together with jujube and āmalaka fruits, / ripe bel fruits, and many diverse roots.
And with venison and various grains, / give satisfaction to the brāhmaṇas through the gift of śrāddha, O you of virtuous vows!
Having reached the forest of Puṣkara, self-restrained and on restricted food, / he who satisfies the ancestors would obtain [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice.
We, however, are going to the eldest Puṣkara for bathing, O Rāma." / Having spoken thus to Rāghava, all those sages departed, O king.
And Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Bring me a sacrificial deer, / and a hare with clear eyes, black vegetables, and honey,
chief lemons, various roots, / and ripe wood-apples, and whatever other fruits there are.
Fetch those quickly for the śrāddha, Lakṣmaṇa!" / And Rāghava did all that according to Rāma's command.
Jujube, ingudī, greens, and various roots: / having gathered them there, a huge heap like a mountain peak was made by Rāma.
And it was cooked thoroughly and prepared by Jānakī, and presented to Rāma. / Having bathed in the Yoga step-well, Rāma waited for those sages.
When the sun had passed midday, at the time of kutapa, / all the ṛṣis who had been invited by Rāma arrived.
Seeing those sages arrived, Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka, / left Rāma's side and, feeling bashful, stood elsewhere,
her eyes wide with wonder, contemplating, and trembling. / The brāhmaṇas did not know that she had withdrawn at the time of the śrāddha.
The brāhmaṇas were fed by Rāma according to the rules declared in the Smṛti, / and all the Vedic rites of hospitality that are prescribed were performed,
as well as the procedure taught in the Purāṇas, preceded by the Vaiśvadeva rite. / When the brāhmaṇas had eaten, having offered rice-balls in due order
and given them sacrificial fees according to his ability, they were dismissed. / When the foremost brāhmaṇas had departed, Rāma said this to his beloved:
"Why did you run away, O fair-browed one, upon seeing the sages arrived here? / Tell me without delay the whole truth of this reason."
"There must be a reason, so do not conceal it from me. / You are adjured by my life and Lakṣmaṇa's, O lady of pure smiles!"
Addressed thus by her husband, standing with face cast down in embarrassment / and shedding tears, she spoke these words to Rāghava:
"Listen, my lord, to the kind of wonder seen here! / While you were meditating, O Rāma, the king of kings arrived here,
along with two others likewise adorned with all ornaments. / Those three entered into the bodies of the twice-born, O scion of Raghu;
the ancestors were seen by me, O Rāghava, within the limbs of the brāhmaṇas. / Seeing them, I was filled with bashfulness and retreated from your presence.
The brāhmaṇas were indeed fed by you, and the śrāddha was performed according to rule. / Clad in bark and deer-skins, how could I appear before the king?
"How could I, O slayer of enemy warriors? This truth is stated. / And the silk garments were taken away by Kaikeyī,
and ever since then I have been clad in bark, sheltered in the forest. / Knowing this, I said nothing, so that you would not feel sorrow.
I do not think of my mother, nor of my father, O scorcher of foes! / 'When will there be an end to this forest dwelling, O Rāghava?'—
As she continuously reflects upon this very thing again and again, O Rāma, / her days pass away, O lord; I swear by your feet.
How could I give this food with my own hand to the king, / [food] such that even a servant of servants would never consume anywhere?
How could one such as I dare to serve him, / I who was formerly seen by the king adorned with every ornament,
holding a whisk in hand and fanning the ruler of men? / Besmeared with sweat and dirt, how could I look upon the king?
Evidently he has attained heaven, delivered by you, his son. / Seeing me, an innocent young woman, grieving and afflicted in the forest,
there would be sorrow for this monarch; because of that I vanished, O Rāghava. / You are as dear to me as life, Rāma; nothing is to be hidden by me from you here.
And in truth of that, I touch your feet." / Hearing that, Rāghava was delighted with his sweet-spoken beloved.
Drawing her to his lap, embracing her firmly and tenderly, / the two heroes then ate the food, and afterwards Jānakī ate.
Remaining thus that night there, the two descendants of Raghu, / when the thousand-rayed sun arose, set their minds on departing.
Going westward for a krośa as far as Jyeṣṭha Puṣkara, / while Rāghava was staying in the eastern part of Puṣkara,
he heard words spoken by a messenger of the gods: / 'O Rāghava! Hail to you! This sacred place is very hard to attain.
Remaining in this place, O hero, make yourself pure! / You must perform the business of the gods; the enemies of the gods are to be slain.'
Then the hero, with a delighted mind, spoke words to Lakṣmaṇa: / 'O Saumitri, I have been favored by the god of gods, Brahmā.
Having made a hermitage site here for one month, O Lakṣmaṇa, / I wish to perform an observance, the supreme purification of the body.'
When Lakṣmaṇa agreed saying 'So be it,' completing the observance, / with gifts such as offering rice balls and with śrāddhas to his forebears,
Rāma then duly made offerings of water to his ancestors at Puṣkara. / Kanakā, Suprabhā, and Nandā, the eastward Sarasvatī,
the five streams in the Puṣkaras that grant satisfaction to the ancestors; / having performed that daily worship of the ancestors beginning with the fathers,
Rāma then said these words to Lakṣmaṇa: / 'Come, Lakṣmaṇa, quickly fetch water from Puṣkara;
having washed our feet, take rest on the bed of grass. / When the night has passed, we will go to the southern region.'
Lakṣmaṇa, however, spoke these words: 'Let the water be brought by Sītā! / I will not be your servant at all times, Rāma!
She is well-nourished, extremely robust, and dear to me as well. / What will you do with this wife? Tell me now!
Or will this beloved of yours follow behind you when you are dead? / You always protect her, well-nourished at all times.
She is joyful, yet constantly troubles me, O best of the Raghus! / And you trouble me, Rāma; in the next world harm will arise [for you].
For your sake I constantly endure thirst together with hunger, / without doubt; and observe the hereafter!
No one is seen following behind those who are dead— / neither wife, nor son, nor wealth; so say the wise.
Your father died, Rāma, leaving behind an unobstructed kingdom / and casting you into the forest to please Kaikeyī.
Here Kaikeyī remained, and the wealth, and all the kinsmen; / the great king Daśaratha went to his destination all alone.
I think Sītā will certainly not go along with you [in death]. / What will you do with her? Tell me now, O Rāghava!'
Hearing the speech spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, never heard before, / Rāghava stood downcast, and so too Sītā of fair countenance.
Whatever Lakṣmaṇa said, Sītā performed it all. / Then the two heroes, with eyes like lotuses, bathed and ate at Puṣkara;
having spent the night there, they set their minds on departing: / 'Come, arise, Saumitri; we will go to the southern region.'
Saumitri said: 'Rāma, I will not go by any means. / Go along with this wife, O lotus-eyed one!
I will not go to another forest, nor to Ayodhyā, O Rāghava; / I will dwell in this forest for fourteen years.
If you do not return to Ayodhyā without me, / then by this path you must return, O king, O lord!
If I am alive at that time, I will go back to my father's city; / I will practice austerities. What will you do with me?
Go, gentle one; auspicious is the path; may there be no highway robbers for you! / May I see you returned again with your wife, O lotus-eyed one!
The ancestral kingdom is in Ayodhyā, O king of men; / both Śatrughna and Bharata abide in carrying out your commands.
I am contrary to you, especially in this forest-dwelling; / ceaselessly by day and by night, O scorcher of foes,
I am unable to do the work. Go happily, gentle one!' / To Saumitri who was speaking thus, the scion of Raghu said:
'How did you set out formerly from Ayodhyā with me, [saying,] / "I will live in the forest, Rāma, for nine and five years;
separated from you, I would not live anywhere, even in heaven; / whatever destination is yours, O tiger among men, that will be mine as well.
Show favor to me, take me also, O Rāghava!" / How can you stay now halfway along the path, O slayer of foes?'
Lakṣmaṇa, however, said to Rāma: 'I will not go into the forest again.' / Knowing Lakṣmaṇa was resolute, Rāma said these words:
'Do not follow me, Saumitri; I will go alone to the forest, / with this Sītā as my second.' Thus spoken to by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa,
taking heed of Rāma's words, then arose; / the two scorchers of foes reached the boundary mountain, the border of the sacred field,
and bowing with eight-limbed prostration before the lord of the gods, Ajagandha, / the god of gods, bearer of the Pināka, the three-eyed one, Rāma [worshiped him].
Standing devoutly, his hair bristling with awe, / joining his palms in supplication, he praised Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī.
Attaining a purely sattvic state, with passion and darkness shaken off, / he recognized the god, the sovereign of the wise, the cause of the worlds.

Rāma said: / He who is the creator of the entire world, moving and unmoving, and gives joy and sorrow for what is done, / and who is also the cause of destruction at the time of the end—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

He who once, upon his head, bore the Gaṅgā falling from the sky like a garland of trembling flowers, / with her pure, lovely, surging waters and rough with great waves—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

When the peak of Mount Kailāsa was violently shaken by the Ten-necked [Rāvaṇa], who resembled a horn of Kailāsa, / it attained stability when held down by his lotus foot—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

By whom the sons of Danu were repeatedly struck down in battle, and hosts of Vidyādharas and Uragas were endowed with all boons, / as were the best of sages living on fruits and roots—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.
Who knocked out Bhaga's eyes at Dakṣa's sacrifice and also the row of Pūṣan's teeth, / and who paralyzed Indra's arm bearing the thunderbolt—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Relying on whom even people who commit sins, whose minds are attached to sensual pleasures, / and who lack the virtues of wisdom, noble lineage, and learning, become enjoyers of bliss—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

The son of Atri [the Moon] whose brilliance equals ten million suns, a terror to the best of gods and Dānavas; / who violently drank the blazing Kālakūṭa poison—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

The lord Maheśa who would grant many a boon to Brahmā, Indra, the Rudras, the Maruts, and the Six-faced [Kārttikeya], / and who rescued Nandi from the jaws of death—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Propitiated with intense asceticism in a bower of the Himālaya through the smoke vow, inaccessible even to the minds of others, / the great soul explained the Saṃjīvanī lore to Bhṛgu—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Who is worshipped by various mighty chiefs of Gaṇas having faces like elephants and cats, the destroyers of Dakṣa's sacrifice, / and by hosts of gods together with the world-protectors—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Who, mounting a noble bull white as a conch, the moon, and jasmine, followed by the daughter of the king of mountains, / traverses the sky adorned with dissolution-clouds—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

When the tranquil sage was being dragged away by those terrifying, dreadful men intent on executing Yama's command, / he bowed in devotion, absorbed in praise, and was forcibly saved by him—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

The god who with the tip of his left lotus-hand's nail violently severed, in the very presence of the gods, / that fifth head of Brahmā, which resembled a fresh lotus—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Bowing with devotion at whose feet, the giver of boons, and praising him with pure words, unwearied in spirit, / the radiant Vivasvat dispels darkness with his rays—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Those foolish men who do not recognize you, the guru of the foremost gods, of this world moving and unmoving, / because of the lingering impression of pride in their mastery of the Vedas, later endure torment, their minds impure.
As he was thus praising him, the bearer of the trident, whose banner is the bull, / delighted, his mind pleased, spoke these words to Rāghava:
Rudra said: / O Rāma, I am pleased, may blessings be upon you! You are born in a spotless race, / and you too are a god deserving the worship of the worlds, having assumed a human form.
With you as their protector, the gods shall indeed be happy for perpetual years; / they will serve [you] for a long time when the fourteenth year has passed.
The mortals on earth who shall see you when you have returned to Ayodhyā / shall enjoy happiness here and an imperishable dwelling in heaven.
Having accomplished a great work for the gods, you may return to the city. / Bowing to the god accordingly, Rāghava departed swiftly.
Reaching the river Indramārgā and fastening his matted locks, / Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: 'Hand me this bow.'
Hearing that word of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Sītā: / 'For what reason, O Queen, have I been abandoned by Rāma without any cause?
I know of no offense, yet the mighty-armed one is angry. / Abandoned by Rāma, I shall undoubtedly give up my life.
I have no need for life! Fie, fie upon me, the defiler of the family, / by whom, a doer of evil, wrath has been aroused in the noble one!
To what worlds shall I go, cursed by the great-souled one?' / Placing both hands over his face, his throat choked with tears, he said this:
'I commit no offense against Rāma in deed, mind, or speech. / I have touched your feet, O Queen; I have no other refuge.'
Then Sītā said to Rāma: 'Why have you abandoned your younger brother? / Let harshness be given up toward the youth Lakṣmaṇa, who increases fortune.'
Rāghava said to Sītā: 'I will not abandon Lakṣmaṇa; / never, even in a dream, is Lakṣmaṇa's intention contrary, my beloved.
And I had heard previously, O fair-hipped one, the working of this sacred place: / in this sacred place, truly, all people are devoted solely to their self-interest.
They do not look out for one another or heed words beneficial to themselves. / Sons do not listen to their father, nor do fathers listen to their sons.
Disciples indeed do not listen to the word of the guru, nor the guru to that of the disciple; / affection is bound up with self-interest, and no one is dear to anyone.'
Speaking thus, the descendant of Kakutstha reached the great river Revā, / and took his ritual bath together with his younger brother and Sītā.
and having gratified his ancestors and deities with libations of water, / composed in mind, he repeatedly looked toward the sun and the deities.
Having performed his bath, Rāma, that king of kings accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, / shone like the blessed Lord Īśa, who has bathed with the Daughter of the Mountain and Guha.

1.34.m: Bhīṣma said: / At what time did the blessed Brahmā, the maker of the world, / begin to sacrifice with sacrificial materials? You should tell that, sir.
What were the names of those officiating priests whom Brahmā appointed? / And what fee was given to them by that great soul?
Recount it to me as it happened and as it came to pass. / A very great curiosity has arisen in me regarding the ancestral sacrifice.
Pulastya said: / It was told by me earlier how Svāyambhuva Manu, / having created all the Prajāpatis, was told: 'Perform creation.'
He himself went to Puṣkara, gathered the array of the sacrifice, / assembled the sacrificial implements, and remained in the fire-sanctuary.
Gandharvas sang constantly, and hosts of Apsarases danced; / the Brahmā, the Udgātṛ, the Hotṛ, and the Adhvaryu were the four bearers of the sacrifice.
And three other assistants were assigned to each one of them by himself: / the Brahmā, the Brahmaṇācchaṃsin, the Potṛ, and the Āgnīdhra.
The inquiry into all knowledge—this is indeed the set of four pertaining to the Brahmā. / The Udgātṛ, the Pratyudgātṛ, the Pratihartṛ, and the Subrahmaṇya:
this is proclaimed as the second set of four, belonging to the Udgātṛ. / The Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, and likewise the Acchāvāka,
and the Grāvastut as the fourth here—this is the third set of four. / The Adhvaryu, the Pratiṣṭhātṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and likewise the Unnetṛ:
this is declared to be the fourth set of four, O son of Śaṃtanu. / These sixteen are indeed proclaimed as priests by the knowers of the Vedas.
Three hundred and sixty sacrifices were created by the Self-born; / and they always appoint these brāhmaṇas for all of them.
Some also require an overseer of the assembly, and an Adhvaryu of the three Sāmans. / He made Nārada the Brahmā, and Gautama the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin;
Devagarbha the Potṛ, and Devala the Āgnīdhra; / Aṅgiras the Udgātṛ, and Pulaha the Pratyudgātṛ;
Nārāyaṇa is called the Pratihartṛ, and Atri the Subrahmaṇya. / In that sacrifice, Bhṛgu was the Hotṛ, and Vasiṣṭha the Maitrāvaruṇa;
Kratu was declared the Acchāvāka, and Cyavana the Grāvastut; / Pulastya was the Adhvaryu, and Śibi the Pratiṣṭhātṛ;
Bṛhaspati was the Neṣṭṛ there, and Śāṃśapāyana the Unnetṛ. / Dharma was the overseer of the assembly there, accompanied by his sons and grandsons.
Bharadvāja, Śamīka, Purukutsa, Yugaṃdhara, / Enaka, Tīrṇaka, Keśa, Kutapa,
Garga, and Vedaśiras were made the Adhvaryus of the three Sāmans; / Kaṇva and others as well, and Mārkaṇḍa and Gaṇḍi,
accompanied by sons and grandsons, with their disciples and kin, / performed the rites there day and night, unwearied.
When a Manvantara had elapsed, the concluding bath of the sacrifice took place. / The eastern direction was given as the priestly fee to the Brahmā, and the southern to the Hotṛ;
the western to the Adhvaryu, and the northern to the Udgātṛ. / Brahmā gave them the entire three worlds as the priestly fee.
And a hundred cows should be given by the wise for the success of the sacrifice; / but forty-eight to the main conductors of the sacrifice;
twenty-four are declared for those of the second rank; / and sixteen auspicious cows should be given to those of the third;
and twelve others he should cause to be given to the Āgnīdhra and the rest. / By this same proportion, villages, female slaves, goats, and sheep,
and food for a thousand should be given after bathing at the concluding bath of the sacrifice. / The sacrificer must give away all his possessions: so spoke the Self-born.
Gifts to the Adhvaryus and the members of the assembly are desired according to one’s wish. / And summoning Viṣṇu, Brahmā, filled with joy, spoke these words:
‘Having propitiated Sāvitrī, bring her here, O you of virtuous vows! / Seeing you, that fair-faced lady will not be angry.
With affectionate, concilatory words, especially reasoned ones; / you always speak sweetly; your tongue distils nectar.
No one who disobeys your word is seen in the three worlds. / Having gone together with the Gandharvas, bring my beloved back.
Propitiated by you, that virtuous, content lady will certainly come. / You must not delay; go, Mādhava, without delay!
Let auspicious Lakṣmī go before you to the abode of Sāvitrī; / follow in her footsteps and console my beloved:
“He does not desire to do anything displeasing to you, O goddess, in secret; / looking at your face, O beautiful lady, he always conducts his life.”
Many such sweet words of this kind / should be made known to the goddess, so that she will soon be pleased.’
Thus spoken to by Brahmā, the creator of the world, Viṣṇu / went quickly to where Sāvitrī was staying.
Seeing Keśava coming with his wife from afar, / she stood up quickly and was saluted by Viṣṇu:
‘Homage to you, O goddess of the ruler of gods! Homage to you, wife of Brahmā! / Having bowed to you, every person is freed from sin.
You are devoted to your husband, most fortunate, dwelling in the heart of Brahmā; / thinking of you day and night, he longs for your favor.
Ask this dear friend, Lakṣmī, the virtuous daughter of Bhṛgu, / if you do not believe my word, O fair-eyed lady!’
Having spoken thus, Śauri then touched both feet of Sāvitrī / with both hands, saying, ‘Forgive, O goddess! Homage to you!’
Touching [her feet], he praised [her], saying, "O one adored by the world, O mother of the world!" / Pulling back her feet with her own hand, the goddess [held] the hands of Hari.
took the hands of Hari and said to Viṣṇu, ‘Everything has been forgiven by me, O Acyuta! / This Lakṣmī, my child, shall always dwell in your heart;
without you she will never find pleasure elsewhere. / Born from the wife of Bhṛgu, this wife of yours is steadfast in her vows;
and by the effort of the gods and demons she was born again from the ocean. / Wherever the Lord is, there she incarnates:
in divinity she indeed has a divine body, and in humanity she is human; / your helper without a doubt, practicing the vow of matrimony forever.
Tell me, O Lord, what I should do here!’ / Viṣṇu said: / ‘The sacrifice has ended; I have been sent to you:
“Bring Sāvitrī quickly; she must perform the bath with me.” / Come quickly, O goddess; go there filled with joy;
having gone, behold your husband joined by all the gods!’ / Lakṣmī said: / ‘O noble lady, arise quickly! Go to where the Grandfather is!
Without you I will not go; your feet have been touched by me.’ / Raising her, she, the capable one, took her right hand in her right hand.
Perceiving that Sāvitrī was delaying, the divine Grandfather / then spoke this word to Mahādeva who was standing nearby:
‘Go together with this Pārvatī, O destroyer of asuras! / Let Gaurī go ahead of you; follow behind, O Śaṃkara.
Reason with her and bring her; do that which will make her come quickly!’ / Thus addressed, the two of them, Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord,
went as directed and spoke to the beloved of Brahmā: / ‘A great duty must be performed by you there, O devoted wife!
Ask this Gaurī of lovely hips, daughter of the mountain, / or this wide-eyed Lakṣmī, or Indrāṇī, O fair-faced lady!
Or ask whichever of them you trust, O goddess! Homage to you!’ / A blessing was given by her to the Trident-bearing god of gods:
‘And Gaurī will always reside in half of your body, O Śaṃkara! / You are adorned by her, O god, and she by you, O handsomest in the three worlds!
The entire world will share in happiness with you as protector, O slayer of foes!’ / As she was speaking thus, Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, was taken
by Gaurī by the left hand, and by Lakṣmī by the right hand. / And having saluted that goddess, Śaṃkara spoke these words:
‘Come, come, O most fortunate lady, to where your husband is! / Go there, O woman of lovely hips! The husband is the supreme refuge of wives.
You ought to go out of love at this great insistence, O goddess! / And this Lakṣmī and Pārvatī are standing before you, O goddess.
By their word, O goddess, and by ours, O fair-faced lady, / it is not fitting for you to maintain wounded pride, O beloved of Brahmā!’

"Besought by us, O goddess, go there filled with joy."

 Gaurī said:
"You always say yourself, O goddess, 'You are dear to me.'

Lakṣmī holds you by one hand, and you are held by me on your right.
Come, O highly fortunate one, to where your husband stands."

She was then led by the two of them, the goddess placed in the middle,
preceded by Viṣṇu and Rudra, and likewise the gods led by Śakra,

and the gandharvas and apsarases, the three worlds with the moving and unmoving.
And the goddess Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, arrived there.

Seeing fair-faced Sāvitrī, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds,
together with Gāyatrī, spoke this word:

"This goddess is your servant; I stand under your control.
Command, O fair-hipped one, whatever deed I must do for you here."

Thus addressed by the god Brahmā himself,
the goddess cast down her face in shame and said nothing at all.

Prompted by Brahmā, the goddess Gāyatrī fell at her feet:
"I have committed an offense against you; forgive me, O goddess, homage to you!"

Embracing her respectfully by the neck, holding close the distressed
Gāyatrī, she consoled her: "He is my respected husband.

His word must be obeyed; for women, the husband is the lord of life.
So was it stated long ago by the blessed Viriñci at the time of creation:

'For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor fasting;
whatever word the husband speaks, she must perform without reproach.'

She who reviles her husband, or likewise reviles his sister,
or slanders or babbles against them, she indeed goes to hell.

While her husband is alive, the woman who performs a vow of fasting
takes away her husband's lifespan, and when dead, she goes to hell.

Knowing this, O virtuous one, you must not do what is displeasing to your husband,
nor must you ever serve his right limb.

In every ritual act, I will abide at his right side;
you should take the left side, O virtuous woman, near Nārada and Puṣkara.

And whatever other sites of Brahmā and temples are established,
I shall surely obtain them, radiant, as long as creation proceeds.

Both you and I must remain; of this there is no doubt.
At Puṣkara, at Brahmā's side, take your place at the left.

And according to this instruction, dwell happily with me."

 Gāyatrī said:
"I will do so, acting upon your instruction.

Your command alone is to be obeyed by me; you are a friend equal to my life.
I am your younger sister, O goddess; you should protect me always."

Then Brahmā, the god of gods, at Puṣkara along with Viṣṇu,
at the conclusion of the bath, granted boons to all the gods:

Śakra as the lord of the gods, the sun as lord of the heavenly lights,
Soma likewise of the lunar mansions, Varuṇa likewise of fluids,

Dakṣa of the Prajāpatis, and the ocean of rivers,
and he made Kubera the lord of wealth, and [ruler] of rakṣasas,

and the wielder of the Pināka [lord] of all ghosts and gaṇas,
Manu of men, and Garuḍa of birds,

Vasiṣṭha of sages, and the radiant sun of planets.
Having bestowed these and other [domains], the grandfather, the god of gods,

Brahmā respectfully spoke to Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara:
"In all the sacred places of the earth, you two are the foremost to be worshipped.
"Without you two, a sacred place never attains holiness, / nor does a liṅga or an icon wherever it is seen."

that sacred place attains holiness and yields all fruits.
Those human beings who will perform worship with offerings

of both of you, placing me first—whence could they fear disease?
In whatever realms the festivals and worships of you both

and all rites are carried out, hear the fruit that exists in them:
there are no mental afflictions or bodily diseases, no harmful visitations, no fear of hunger,

no separation from loved ones, nor union with the disliked,
no eye disease or headache, bile disorders, acute pain, or fistula,

no sorcery, no fear there, no epilepsy, nor cholera;
there is abundant prosperity and an unexcelled, sound intellect,

complete health on every side, long life, offspring, and wealth;
death will not occur prematurely; cows will not yield little milk;

trees will not bear fruit out of season; and there will not be the slightest danger from portents."
Hearing this, Viṣṇu then set about praising Brahmā.

Viṣṇu said:
"Homage to the endless one of pure mind, whose form is your essential nature, of a thousand arms,
the creator who is the source of a thousand rays of light, of vast body, of pure deeds!

Homage to Śambhu who removes the distress of the whole universe, whose fiery splendor equals all suns and fires!
Homage to the one spread throughout knowledge, the discus-wielder; homage always to the author of all intellect's abodes!

O beginningless god, Lord whose crest is Acyuta, Lord of beings past, present, and future, O Great Lord,
Lord of the great, Lord of all, Lord of the world, Lord of the earth, Lord of creation, homage always to you!

O Lord of sacrifice, Nārāyaṇa, Jiṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Lord of the earth, Lord of the universe, all-seeing eye,
moon, sun, Acyuta, hero, cosmic form manifested, embodied and unembodied, imperishable!

O Nārāyaṇa whose realm's regions are blocked by blazing flames of sacrificial fire, facing everywhere,
remover of the distress of all the gods, immortal, imperishable—protect me, O Lord, who have thus sought your refuge!

I behold your manifold faces, O Lord, the ancient course of sacrifice,
Brahmā, the Lord, the origin of the worlds; homage to you, the great-grandfather!

Through the many revolutions of the wheel of saṃsāra, somewhere you are the supreme god among the best of gods;
you are worshipped by those whose natures are purified through all discernment—how shall I bow down to you?

He who knows you thus, prior to primordial nature, is the foremost of all who know;
you are to be forcibly discerned among those endowed with qualities, vast of form, yet subtle in form here.

Though destitute of the organs of speech, hands, and feet, how indeed are you the good refuge and the doer of good deeds?
Though your senses are placed in the bondage of saṃsāra, how again are you the best of gods to be known?

The unmanifest is not obtained from the manifest, nor the higher body, O god, except by those of pure dispositions
who offer sacrifice, cutting off saṃsāra; therefore this four-faced nature of yours is assumed.

Since even the gods do not know your higher body, O bearer of wonderful form,
one should worship your ancient form, which is foremost among your manifestations, seated upon a lotus seat.

Even the creator of the universe does not know your essence; only one who knows the single origin, pure in disposition, [knows].
Yet how can I know you, the ancient, the primordial one, purified by ascetic heat?

The lotus-seated one is celebrated as the progenitor; such is the renown repeatedly from the Purāṇa.
One contemplates you, O Lord, all-pervading; one destitute of ascetic heat does not know you thus.

You, O god, who are to be discerned by foremost beings like us, fools dividing their own intellects
wish to understand; there is no wisdom in them, even among those of noble fame, who are devoid of the Veda.

If illumination should come through the intellect that discerns the Veda across other births,
for one eager for that attainment, human birth is not adequate, nor would he become a god, a lord of gandharvas, or Śiva.

You are not of Viṣṇu's form; you, O blessed one, are very subtle; yet you are gross, O god, because your purpose is accomplished.
Though gross, you are subtle, easy to attain, O god; those whose acts are alienated from you fall into hell."

Or is one liberated, when He remains in this [body], / possessing an extended nature in His own self, holding identical forms by means of the elements, the self-forms: the [two] Aśvins, the moon, fire, the sun, the wind, and the earth?
"O Lord, accept this hymn of mine, O Endless One, and especially of your devotee, / who is endowed with meditation, of purified mind, whose mind solely follows contemplation of your nature."
Dwelling always in the heart, O Lord, homage to You; I bow down always, O ancient Lord. / Thus this hymn of Yours has been revealed by me, O Lord, who are awakened to all paths.
Protect us again from fear / accompanied by wandering in the wheel of worldly existence.

Brahmā said:
You are omniscient, there is no doubt, and a heap of wisdom, O Keśava. / You shall always be the first to be worshiped among the gods.
Immediately after Nārāyaṇa, Rudra with devotion / praised Viriñci, Brahmā born from a lotus, bowing down:
Homage, O lotus-petal-eyed one! Homage to You born from a lotus! / Homage, O teacher of gods and asuras, O agent, O supreme Self!
Homage to You, O Lord of all gods! Homage indeed, O destroyer of delusion, / who abide in Viṣṇu's navel, whose birth is the lotus-seat!
Homage to You who have limbs red like coral, shining with hands like tender shoots! / I have sought refuge in You; save me from worldly existence!
Formerly, having seen a bud shaped like a dark cloud, / and then a red tip endowed with petals and filaments, O Grandfather,
and an untainted lotus with numerous petal-tips, beyond number, / standing upon it, this creation was set in motion by You.
"Except for you, there is no protection elsewhere, O you adored by the world, homage to you! / I am burnt by the curse of Sāvitrī; my liṅga has fallen upon the earth."
Now grant peace to me, and save me together with my wife. / May Brahmā protect my feet, and may the Lotus-seated protect my shanks.
May Viriñci protect my waist, and the Creator of creation my private parts; / may the Lotus-like protect my navel, and the Four-faced my belly.
May the Maker of the universe protect my chest, and the Lotus-born protect my heart; / may the husband of Sāvitrī protect my throat, and Hṛṣīkeśa my face.
May the Lotus-colored protect my eyes, and the supreme Self my head. / Having thus applied the name of the teacher, Śaṅkara, causing auspiciousness [to the name],
having said: 'Homage to You, O Lord Brahmā!', he ceased. / Then Brahmā, pleased, spoke this sentence to Hara:
What desire of yours shall I grant today? Ask me whatever you wish. / Rudra said: / If You are pleased with me, O Lord, or if You are a granter of boons to me,
tell me that one thing, O all-pervading Lord: in which place do You abide, / and in which places do the twice-born always behold You?
And by what name is Your dwelling adorned on the surface of the earth? / Tell that to me, who am devoted to Your worship, O Lord of all!

Brahmā said:
In Puṣkara I am the Best of Gods, and in Gayā the Four-faced; / in Kānyakubja the Womb of the Gods, in Bhṛgukakṣa the Grandfather;
at the Kāverī the Creator of Creation, and in Nandipurī Bṛhaspati; / in Prabhāsa the Lotus-born, and in Vānarī the Beloved of Gods;
in Dvāravatī the Knower of the Ṛgveda, in Vaidiśa the Ruler of the World; / in Pauṇḍraka the Lotus-eyed, in Hastināpura the Yellow-eyed;
in Jayantī I am Vijaya, and Jayanta in Puṣkarāvatī; / among the Ugras I am Lotus-handed, at the river Tamā the Dispeller of Darkness;
in Ahicchatra Jayānandin, in the city of Kāñcī Beloved of the People; / I am Brahmā in Pāṭaliputra, and the Sage in Ṛṣikuṇḍa;
in Mahitāra Mukunda, and Śrīkaṇṭha in Śrīnivāsita; / in Kāmarūpa possessing an auspicious form, in Vārāṇasī beloved of Śiva;
likewise in Mallikākṣa Viṣṇu, on Mahendra the descendant of Bhṛgu; / in Gonarda having the form of an elder, in Ujjayinī the Grandfather;
in Kauśāmbī the Great Awakened One, and in Ayodhyā Rāghava; / on Citrakūṭa the Lord of Sages, and the Boar on the Vindhya mountain;
at Gaṅgādvāra the Supreme Deity, and on the Himavat Śaṅkara; / at the Devikā holding a ladle, and holding an offering-ladle at Caturvaṭa;
in Vṛndāvana Lotus-handed, and holding kuśa-grass at Naimiṣa; / at Goplakṣa Lord of the Cowherds, and accompanied by the moon on the bank of the Yamunā;
on the Bhāgīrathī Lotus-bodied, and Jalānanda in Jalandhara; / in Koṅkaṇa Madrākṣa, and in Kāmpilya Fond of Gold;
at Veṅkaṭa Giver of Food, and Śambhu at Kratusthala; / in Laṅkā Pulastya, and in Kaśmīra the Swan-vehicled;
Vasiṣṭha on Arbuda, and Nārada in Utpalāvatī; / at Melaka I am Giver of the Veda, and at the waterfall Lord of Aquatic Creatures;
likewise the Sāmaveda at the sacrifice, Fond of Sweetness in Mathurā; / in Aṅkoṭa the Enjoyer of the Sacrifice, and in Brahmavāda Beloved of the Gods;
Nārāyaṇa on Gomanta, and Beloved of the Twice-born in Māyāpurī; / in Ṛṣiveda Invincible, and in Devā Destroyer of the Asuras;
in Vijayā Having a Great Form, Having His Own Form in Rāṣṭravardhana; / Broad-bellied in Mālavyā, and Fond of Flavor in Śākambharī;
Gopāla at Piṇḍāraka, Increasing Limbs at Śaṅkhoddhāra; / Overseer of Creatures in Kādambaka, Overseer of Gods in Samasthala;
Gaṅgādhara at Bhadrapīṭha, and I am Sleeping on the Waters on Arbuda; / Ruler of Tripura at Tryambaka, and Three-eyed on Śrīparvata;
Mahādeva in Padmapura, and the Son of Vidhi in Kāpāla; / Śauri in Śṛṅgaverapura, and Disc-handed in Naimiṣa;
Uneven-eyed in Daṇḍapurī, Gautama at Dhūtapāpa; / Lord of Swans on Mālyavat, and Chief of the Twice-born in Valikā;
Lord of Gods in Indrapurī, Purandara in Dyūtapā; / Carried by a Swan in Lambā, and Fond of Garuḍa in Caṇḍā;
Great Sacrifice in Mahodaya, Having Good Sacrifices in Yajñaketana; / Lotus-colored in Siddhismara, Awakener of the Lotus in Vibhā;
the Liṅga in Devadāruvana, Vināyaka in Mahāpatti; / Tryambaka at the abode of the Mothers, and Head of the Family in Alakā;
Gonarda on Trikūṭa, and Vāsuki in Pātāla; / Preserver of the Lotus at Kedāra, Fond of Sexual Union in Kūṣmāṇḍa;
Having Auspicious Limbs at Kuṇḍavāpī, and Takṣaka in Sāraṇī; / Remover of Sins in Akṣoṭa, and Sudarśana in Ambikā;
Great Hero at the Varadā, Destroyer of Difficulties in the forest; / Ananta in Parṇāṭa, and the Sun in Prakāśā;
Lotus-navelled in Virajā, and His Own Rudra in Vṛkasthala; / Mārkaṇḍa at Vaṭaka, and Having a Deer as His Banner at the Vāhinī;
Having a Lotus Abode in Padmāvatī, Having a Lotus Banner in the sky. / One hundred and eight places have been recounted to you by me,
where indeed is my presence at the three junctions of the day, O Destroyer of Tripura. / A devout person who sees even one of these,
having attained a completely pure station, rejoices for eternal years. / Whatever misdeed of mind, of speech,
and of body—all that comes to destruction; no deliberation is to be made on this. / And that man who, having gone to all these, beholds me,
becomes a sharer in liberation, where I indeed abide. / By offerings of flowers and incenses, and by gratifications of brāhmaṇas,
and by steady meditation, the Supreme Lord is swiftly attained. / His is the highest fruit of merit, and in the end the fruit of liberation likewise;
having reached the world of Brahmā, he remains there for that time; / at creation again, he will be a god of the Vairājas, of great austerity.
Even sins such as killing a Brahmin committed in this world, / whether unintentionally or intentionally, perish in an instant.
Whoever is poor in this world, or has fallen from his kingdom, / goes to these places and beholds me with concentrated meditation,
and performs worship with offerings, bathing, and libations to the ancestors, / and makes an offering of rice-balls, he is soon freed from suffering.
He will become a sole sovereign king; this is the truth, there is no doubt. / Kingdoms in this world, good fortune, wealth, grain, and excellent women
of various kinds come to him who has made the pilgrimage to Puṣkara. / Whoever performs this pilgrimage rite or causes it to be performed,
or hears it, is indeed freed from all sins. / If a man knows that he has approached a forbidden woman,
or that Vedic rites have been neglected for many years, / having made this pilgrimage once, he will attain Vedic purification.
What is the use of saying much here? This is the case here, O Śaṅkara: / by it the unattainable is attained, and even sin is destroyed.
It is equal to the fruits of all sacrifices, granting the fruit of all holy fords; / indeed, through it the completion of all the Vedas is accomplished.
By those who, having performed the twilight worship at Puṣkara, have revered Sāvitrī / with Puṣkara water presented by their own wife's hand,
with an excellent water-pot, even an earthen one, O Śaṅkara, / that holy water having been brought, twilight worship at the end of the day
is to be performed with concentrated meditation, preceded by breath control. / Listen now to me, O Hara, about the merit gained when that is performed:
by that, twilight worship would be praised as performed for twelve years. / The fruit of a horse sacrifice is gained by bathing, and tenfold by giving gifts;
and by fasting, it is endless; this was declared by me myself, O sinless one. / Whoever gives food to a married couple before Sāvitrī,
by that I am fed there in this world, without a doubt. / Whoever feeds a second [couple], by him Keśava is fed;
accompanied by Lakṣmī, the boon-granting lord bestows boons upon him. / If a third is fed, you yourself, accompanied by Umā, are fed, no doubt.
Or she who gives food to young maidens with devotion / will never have a barren or unfortunate woman in her family.
nowhere will a woman give birth only to daughters, nor will she be unloved by her husband. / Therefore, with all effort, food before Sāvitrī
should always be given by men desiring [fruits] in the next world or in this world, / always free from pungent oil, O Bhīṣma,
and neither sour nor alkaline food should ever be given to women; / [give] food of five kinds, well prepared with all the flavours,
well-cooked ghee-cakes filled with abundant milk, / and likewise the drink *śikhariṇī*, mixed with curds and milk,
delightful to men and exceedingly beloved to women, / endowed with wealth, grain, and [attendant] people, and crowded with a hundred women.
cakes and crisp pastries are produced for her, of this there is no doubt; / there is neither fever, nor torment, nor sorrow, nor separation.
She delivers twenty-one generations of her own family; / accompanied by kinsmen, sons, and countless servant maids and men,
and her family is filled [with abundance], she who gives fried pastry-cakes; / and she thrives for a long time together with sons and grandsons.
The entire family of him who gives crisp pastries [thrives]; / their daughters indeed bear sons, and the family is united with kinsmen.
Of the young women who bestow *śikhariṇī*, there is no doubt / that her family rejoices, filled with every success.
By giving sweetmeat-balls—thus spoke Prajāpati— / precisely this food of young girls is praised, O Hara.
Fortunate, possessing sons, virtuous, endowed with wealth and prosperity, / she will be one who feeds a thousand in birth after birth, O Śambhu.
And holy cakes, prepared sweet, / with grape-juice prominent and combined with pieces of jaggery,
having mixed pieces [of jaggery] with autumnal grain, / should be drinks for women and food for twice-born men.
And here, woolen garments suitable for the rainy season of all kinds, / and whatever drinks are suitable, those he should cause to be given;
having honoured them according to the rule with gifts of wealth and with bodices, / their limbs smeared with saffron, adorned with garlands of flowers,
having given shoes for the feet and a coconut in the hand, / and having applied collyrium to the eyes and vermilion to the head,
having placed in their hands jaggery, delightful and desired soft fruits, / along with vessels, having bowed down, he should send them off.
He himself should eat afterwards, with his kinsmen and children. / Or, if there is no wealth at the holy ford for giving and feeding,
"Having gone home, I will give; be pleased with me, O delighted God!" / In this very way, for the ancestors, having returned to his own abode,
he should perform the ancestral rite according to rule, preceded by the offering of rice-balls; / his ancestors become satisfied until the end of a day of Brahmā.
The merit of those who give in their own home is eight times that of a holy ford, O Śiva; / and the base do not see the ancestral rite performed by the twice-born.
The ancestral rite for the ancestors is prescribed in solitude in a secluded home; / ruined by the gaze of the low, it does not reach the ancestors.
Therefore, with all effort, one should have the ancestral rite performed in secret; / it is declared to give satisfaction to the ancestors by the Self-born himself.
That which is [performed] with intense devotion to Gaurī is praised as a known ritual; / that known through a passionate mind brings fame to people.
A gift should always be given in secret by one desiring one's own welfare; / when cooked food is given by people on earth, let it be seen:
what is seen is for their satisfaction, but it should not be seen here at any time. / When one Brahmin is fed, ten million are fed;
by this becoming so, there is no doubt: true is the Purāṇic word. / But at a holy ford, one should never examine a Brahmin.
Manu declared that any suppliant who has arrived there should be fed. / The offering of rice-balls with barley-meal, with festive wheat cakes, or with rice boiled in milk,
is to be performed, as seen by the sages, or with oil-cake or the *iṅguda* fruit; / it should always be given with sesame oil-cakes by devoted men.
The ancestral rite is to be performed there without offering water for the hands or invocation; / vultures and crows do not take away that funeral offering by their gaze.
That ancestral rite is declared to belong to the holy ford, giving supreme satisfaction to the ancestors; / it should be performed with effort: devotion alone is the cause here.
The ancestors are pleased through devotion; pleased, they bestow desires: / a son, a grandson, wealth, grain, and whatever desires one wishes in one's mind.

Worshipped with devotion, the pleased grandfather would bestow [desires] upon men. / Whether at an improper time or at a proper time, an ancestral rite at a holy ford [should be performed] by men always;
having merely arrived, bathing and libations to ancestors should always be performed, / and the offering of rice-balls, exceedingly dear to the ancestors, should be performed.
For the ancestors look out for a descendant of the lineage who has arrived; / endowed with the highest hope, they yearn for water from him.
Delay should not be made, nor should one cause an obstacle; / unbroken their lineage will be for all time.
The ancestors are the givers of sons, desiring the ancestral rite of prosperity; / therefore they never cause an interruption of lineage.
Therefore, śrāddha was spoken of of old by the Self-born one himself, / which, supreme in merits, must be performed by twice-born men devoted to the ancestors,
at a sacred ford, a sacred field, or at home; at a solar transit or an eclipse; / at an equinox, a solstice, or when one's birth constellation is afflicted.
These indeed the son of the Self-born declared of old to be the times for śrāddha. / When a śrāddha is performed, men suffer no bodily affliction;
then all wrong deeds, even those committed by a son, depart, / so that no affliction will arise from planets, thieves, kings, and the like.
All wrong deeds perish, and in the next world he attains an auspicious destination; / there is no doubt about this, according to the word of Prajāpati.

In the Kṛta age Puṣkara is remembered, in the Tretā age Naimiṣa,
and in the Dvāpara age Kurukṣetra; in the Kali age one should resort to the Gaṅgā.

Dwelling at Puṣkara is difficult to perform; asceticism at Puṣkara is difficult to perform.
Whatever sin is committed elsewhere becomes lightened at a sacred site;

A sin committed at a sacred site is not removed anywhere else.
Whoever remembers Puṣkara with folded hands at evening and morning,

by him ablution has been performed at all sacred sites, O Bhārata.
Having performed ablution at Puṣkara morning and evening with senses restrained,

one obtains all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā.
For twelve years, twelve days, a month, or even half a month,

whoever resides continually at Puṣkara goes to the supreme state.
Above all the worlds stands the world of Brahmā.

He who wishes to go to Puṣkara should attend upon Puṣkara.
Just as in regular and reverse order, so in separate and combined parts,

having bathed properly at Puṣkara, one enjoys the fruit of ten million [sacred baths].
Whatever fruit is [found] in all the sacred sites being visited according to rule,

a man obtains that fruit merely by beholding Puṣkara.
There are indeed one hundred million sacred sites on the earth's surface;

their presence is at Puṣkara at the three junctions of the day, O joy of the Kurus.
As long as mountains stand, as long as oceans stand,

so long is the world of Brahmā for those who die at Puṣkara, there is no doubt.
And through thousands of other births, from birth until the end of death,

one burns away all evil deeds having bathed just once at Puṣkara.
Puṣkara is a sacred place difficult of access, destroying all sins.

Now hear from me, O king, about the worship destroying the five great sins,
of the God of gods, granting the world of Brahmā, sons, and wealth.

Whatever man on earth is afflicted in this life with poverty, sickness, leprosy, and the like,
and is destitute of fortune and childless,

his fortune immediately appears, with full lifespan, sons, and happiness.
Having set him in a maṇḍala accompanied by the guardians of the world,

whoever beholds according to rule Brahmā, the supreme god,
worshipped with a nine-naved design, the embodiment of mantras, not born from a womb,

especially on the full-moon day in the bright half of the month of Kārtika,
or worships the god according to rule on every full-moon day,

or at a solstitial transit, O mighty-armed one, or at an eclipse of the moon or sun,
whoever beholds the all-pervading god worshipped by the guru, O king,

his satisfaction arises immediately, and destruction of sins takes place;
and he becomes equal to the gods in this world, O ruler of men.

The guru should test the devoted Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas
for a year by means of their caste, purity, actions, and the like.

Having understood them to be qualified, he should resolve [so] in his heart.
They too, endowed with devotion, having meditated on the teacher as the Supreme Lord,

should show devotion to the guru for a year just as to Viṣṇu.
Then, when the year is complete, they should propitiate the guru:

"O Lord, by your grace comes crossing the ocean of saṃsāra,
by the contemplation of the Supreme Brahman and the propitiation of Viriñci,

by the recitation of the Puruṣasūkta, by the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa,
and by meditation; so let instruction be given to us.

We desire Vedic fortune; especially be pleased!"
Being thus requested by them, the wise guru then,

having properly worshipped Brahmā with Viṣṇu in front,
should have them lie down blindfolded on the fourteenth of Kārtika.

Rising in the Brahmamuhūrta, having assumed the lotus posture,
having meditated on the guru in the thousand-petaled lotus, wearing white garments and sacred thread,

wearing white garlands and clothes, anointed with white sandal paste,
and having gone outside to a river, they should perform their daily rites unwearied.

The teacher should give a tooth-stick derived from a milky tree,
and having gone to a river flowing to the ocean, they should chew it,

or at another [water body], or a tank, or even at home according to rule;
they should chew it consecrated with the mantra of Parameṣṭhin.

Consecrated seven times with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā",
having recited "devasya tvā", he should place it in the hand with "yuñjānaḥ".

Having washed it with "irāvatī", [and chewed it] in the mouth with "brahmodana",
having chewed it, he should throw it far away and observe it as it falls:

whether it has fallen facing forward, facing east, or toward an intermediate direction.
Facing forward, there is attainment of the deity and accomplishment of the mantra;

if the tooth-stick faces away, all the gods face away;
if it falls to the north, success may or may not occur;

to the south, there will be death for the guru, there is no doubt.
Having seen the auspicious, he should sleep on the ground near the God of gods.

Having seen dreams, the wise [disciples] should recount them before the guru;
then the supreme guru should discern the auspicious and inauspicious therein.

Then on the full-moon day, having bathed, one should go to the temple of the god.
And the guru should trace a maṇḍala on the prepared ground,

having marked the ground with various characteristics according to rule;
the wise one should draw a sixteen-spoked lotus, or one with nine sections,

or having drawn an eight-petaled one, he should show it.
He should carefully bind their eyes with a white cloth.

He should lead the disciples, holding flowers in their hands, inside in order of their caste.
When the wise one makes a nine-naved maṇḍala with powders,

he should worship the god Indra, preceded by Indrāṇī, in the east;
similarly, O king, he should worship Agni together with the guardians of the world,

in the direction of Fire; Yama in the south; and Nirṛti in the southwest;
Varuṇa in the direction of Varuṇa; Vāyu in the realm of the northwest;

placing Dhanada in the north, and Rudra in the realm of Īśāna;
the waterpot in the east, and the sacrificial ladle in the south;

the goose in the west, and the dipping-spoon in the north;
he should place the sacred seat in the southeast, and the sandals in the southwest,

the meditation-band in the northwest, and the water-dropper in the northeast.
Viṣṇu is to be worshipped in the east, and Śaṃkara in the south,

the sun-god in the west, and the sages in the north.
In the center is the Lotus-born himself, with Sāvitrī on his right,

and in the north goddess Gāyatrī, with eyes like lotus petals.
Placing the Ṛgveda in the east, and the Yajurveda in the south,

the Sāmaveda in the west, and the Atharvaveda in the north,
as well as the legendary histories, Purāṇas, prosody, and astronomy,

and other Dharmaśāstras, he should arrange them in the directions beginning with Indra.
Having worshipped Bala on the eastern petal, Pradyumna on the southern petal,

Aniruddha in the west, and Vāsudeva in the north;
Vāmadeva in the east, and Sadyojāta in the south;

having placed Īśāna in the west, and Tatpuruṣa in the north;
Aghora is to be worshipped in every direction: this is the worship in the maṇḍala.

Having worshipped Bhāskara in the east, Divākara in the south,
Prabhākara in the west, and the King of Planets in the north;

having thus worshipped Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, according to rule,
and having arranged eight water-jars in the circle of directions according to rule,

he should prepare a ninth jar dedicated to Brahmā in the center.
He should bathe one desiring liberation with the jar of Brahmā;

one desiring prosperity with the Vaiṣṇava jar, O king;
and he should bathe one seeking a kingdom with the jar dedicated to Indra.
One desiring wealth and radiance [should bathe a man] with the water of the jar of Agni; / to conquer death through the rite, one should bathe a man with [the jar] of Yama.
It is prescribed [to bathe] with [the jar] of Nirṛti enough to utterly destroy the wicked; / one should bathe a man quickly with [the jar] of Varuṇa for the destruction of sin.
One desiring bodily health should be consecrated with [the jar] of Vāyu; / [a bath] with [the jar] of Kubera is prescribed for one desiring an abundance of wealth.
For one desiring knowledge, with [the jar] of Rudra. These are the jars of the World Guardians; / having bathed with each one, a man is freed from all defects.
Whether a king or an ordinary man, he becomes like Brahmā at once. / Or else, one should worship the World Guardians in all the cardinal directions according to their sequence,
by their own names, using the jars according to the ritual rule. / Having thus worshipped the gods, the World Guardians, with a clear mind,
he should then bring inside the tested disciples, their eyes blindfolded; / having burned [their impurities] through the fiery concentration, he should then scatter them by the wind.
Having nourished them with soma, he should then have them listen to the pledges: / 'One must not revile Brahmins, the gods, Viṣṇu, nor Brahmā,
nor Indra, the Sun, Fire, the World Guardians, and the planets, / nor the guru, or a Brahmin, or an eminent sage who has been initiated before.'
Having thus recited the pledges, he should then perform the fire sacrifice: / 'Oṃ, homage to the blessed Brahmā, who possesses all forms, huṃ phaṭ svāhā.'
With this sixteen-syllable mantra, he should offer oblations into the blazing fire; / he should cause all the oblations, beginning with conception, to be offered,
with the three sacred utterances in the presence of the God of Gods. / At the end of the fire sacrifice, the initiate should then give a sacrificial fee to the guru.
Elephants, horses, vehicles, carts, gold, grain, and the like, O king, / the wise man should give to the guru; if middling, then middling [gifts].
In other cases, he should give a pair [of garments] along with gold to that guru. / When this is done, the great religious merit that is produced—
it is impossible to describe that even in hundreds of years. / If one has first become an initiate and then listens to the Padma Purāṇa,
by him the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and all mantras with their compendia / would be chanted at the sacred bath of Puṣkara, at Prayāga, at the confluence of the ocean and the Sindhu,
at the Devahrada lake, at Kurukṣetra, and especially at Vārāṇasī. / Whatever fruit belongs to those who recite during an eclipse and an equinox,
and that fruit multiplied a hundredfold, having seen the Grandfather abiding at Puṣkara, / he attains, and various desires if he desires them.
The initiated one who performs ritual worship and listens [to it]— / even the gods, having performed asceticism, meditate and say:
'When will my birth occur in the land of Bhārata, O king? / When shall we become initiates and listen to the Padma Purāṇa?
And when, having placed the sixteen-formed Padma Purāṇa upon our bodies, / shall we go to the supreme abode, having gone to which one does not return?'
Thus the gods speak and ponder in their minds: / 'And when, O king, shall we behold the sacrifice to Brahmā on the full moon of Kārttika?'
Thus this ritual has been explained to you by me, O best of Kurus; / for this is always difficult to obtain even for gods, gandharvas, and yakṣas.
He who knows this in truth, and he who sees the maṇḍala, / and he who hears this—all are liberated; such is the sacred revelation.
Beyond this, I shall declare this supreme secret, / by which prosperity, fortitude, contentment, and nourishment come to mortals,
and by which all the planets always become gentle, O king. / First undertaking [the vow] on a Sunday under the Hasta nakṣatra with devotion,
he should pass the time with one meal until seven in number; / then, when the seventh is completed, he should feed Brahmins.
And having carefully made a golden image of the Sun, a man / should cover it with a pair of red garments, and an umbrella and shoes,
and sandals are to be given; he should place it in a copper vessel. / Having bathed it with ghee, [he should give it] to a Brahmin whose limbs are complete;
he should give it particularly to a Brahmin who knows the ritual duties. / When this is done, his fruit will be excellent health,
and the attainment of complete wealth—such is the Purāṇic rite. / And this [rite] is unfailing, bestowing peace and nourishment upon mortals.
Likewise, undertaking [the vow] on a Monday under the Citrā nakṣatra, the wise man, / eating only at night, should carefully pass eight Mondays.
On each one, wise Brahmins are to be fed according to one's capacity; / and then, when the ninth is completed, he should feed Brahmins.
A pair of garments is to be given, and then he should donate [an image of] the Moon / placed in a bronze vessel that is filled with milk;
likewise an umbrella, shoes, and equipped with sandals, / it should be given especially to a Brahmin whose limbs are complete.
Having worshipped Mars under the Svātī nakṣatra, he should pass [the days] with night-time meals; / thus up to eight [times], and he should feed Brahmins.
And a golden [image of] Mars placed in a copper vessel / he should then give to a Brahmin, and indeed to one whose limbs are complete.
In the order of the nakṣatras, he should pass seven night [fasts]; / on the eighth, in order, the wise man should give golden planetary images.
And he should perform the fire ritual according to the rule as seen [in scripture]. / When this is done, whatever happens, learn that, O lord of men!
All the ungentle planets also become gentle in form, / all diseases vanish, and the deities attain satisfaction.
The serpent spirits do not obstruct him, the ancestors are gratified, / and destruction of bad dreams occurs for those who listen and those who recite.
If Mars, Saturn, the Sun along with Rāhu, / and Ketu stand at the zenith—the fierce planets that cause affliction—
merely by having performed this, they become auspicious. / The one who performs this thus, O king, always endowed with devotion,
to him they are all gracious and grant peace; it is not otherwise. / One should place Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu in iron vessels;
one should have them made of iron and give them to Brahmins. / A pair of black garments is to be given to propitiate them,
and golden limbs are to be given by those desiring peace, prosperity, and victory. / At the conclusion of the vow, all these planets are golden, O king,
and are to be given by those desiring peace; at the end of the vow, feeding of the twice-born / and a fee according to one's capacity, for the pleasing of the planets.
With little effort, O king of kings, one will obtain all desires. / One should seek knowledge from Śiva, and health from the Sun;
one should seek wealth from Fire, and the [highest] destination from Janārdana; / and the status of Brahmā from the Grandfather, which brings peace to all living beings.
Bhīṣma said: / The sacrifice described by you indeed brings great fruit to sacrificers; / but because of the brevity of life, it cannot be attained by others.
Whatever great fruit of merit arises from fasting for a year / with little effort, tell me that, O best of sages!
Pulastya said: / For this purpose, O great king, the renowned King Śveta, / afflicted intensely by hunger, asked a question of Vasiṣṭha.
In the Ilāvṛta continent, there was a mighty king named Śveta; / he conquered the whole earth together with its seven continents and cities.
And Vasiṣṭha, the mind-born son of Brahmā, was his family priest. / Once, that best of kings, having conquered [the earth], supremely righteous,
He said this to his family priest, Vasiṣṭha, best among reciters of prayers. / Śveta said: / 'O lord, I am eager to perform a thousand horse sacrifices,
and to give gifts of gold, silver, and jewels to twice-born men; / but gifts of food on earth, O guru, I truly do not wish to give.
Nothing [lasts] through food given in a sacrifice or to a twice-born, O lord; / knowing it to be an ephemeral thing, it was never given.'
Red garments, ornaments, villages, and towns / that highly renowned King Śveta gave to the brāhmaṇas.
Neither food nor water was ever given by that king. / Then, having sacrificed with many horse sacrifices, that best of kings,
having practiced austerities for three hundred million [years], went to heaven won by merit; / adorned with all ornaments, he attained the world of Brahmā.
There apsarases danced, and women of the siddhas sang; / both Tuṃburu and Nārada were always in his attendance there.
The two exceedingly wise ones sang, and sages endowed with austerity / praised with mantras uttered in the Veda him who had offered many sacrifices.
Yet although the great-souled king was endowed with such glory, / his body was afflicted by hunger, and especially by thirst.
Tormented by that hunger, that best of kings / left heaven in his aerial chariot and went to the Ṛkṣa mountain.
He went to where his own physical body had of old been burned in the great forest; / taking his own bones there, that ruler of the earth sat licking them.
Mounting his aerial chariot again, the lord of men went to heaven. / Then after a long time, that king of strict vows
was seen licking his own bones by Vasiṣṭha, his family priest, / and addressed: 'Why, O king of kings, O ruler of men, are you eating your own bones?'
Thus addressed by the great sage Vasiṣṭha, / King Śveta then spoke this word to that sage:
'O venerable one, I am afflicted with thirst and hunger. In the past, the gift of food / was not given by me, O tiger among sages; therefore hunger oppresses me.'
When the king had spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha, the eminent sage, / that great sage spoke once again to the king these words:
'What shall I do for you, O king of kings, who are particularly hungry? / Surely nothing ever comes to anyone which was not given [by him].
By giving jewels and gold, a man becomes an enjoyer of pleasures; / by giving gifts of food, he is illumined with all desires fulfilled.
That was not given by you, O king, thinking it to be insignificant.' / Śveta said: / 'How may the production of what was not given occur for me, O guru?
By your favor, O Vasiṣṭha, declare that to me who am asking.' / Vasiṣṭha said: / 'There is one means by which it comes to be; of this there is no doubt.
Listen to that, O tiger among men, as it is being told by me to you. / In a previous age there was a king known as Vinītāśva.
That excellent king undertook to perform a horse sacrifice; / at the end of the sacrifice, what was requested—cows, horses, and the like—was given to the best of twice-born.
No food was given by him, thinking it trifling, just as by you. / Then after a long time, he died on the bank of the Jāhnavī.
In Māyāpurī, Vinītāśva had been a universal emperor; / and he too went to heaven, just as you have, O king, O lord.
Overcome by hunger, he too went just so / to the world of mortals, to the bank of the river, to the Gaṅgā at the Nīla mountain.
In an aerial chariot bright as the sun, shining like a god, O king, / he saw his own body, and likewise his own family priest,
a brāhmaṇa, the Hotṛ priest, sacrificing on the bank of the Jāhnavī. / Seeing him, he in turn asked that best of the twice-born
the cause of his hunger, O king; and that Hotṛ priest said to him: / 'A sesame-cow, O king, and a ghee-cow, O best of men,
a water-cow, a milk-cow, and a juice-cow, O ruler of the earth, / give quickly, so that you may be free of thirst and hunger in heaven,
and may rejoice as long as the sun and the moon shine in the sky.' / Being addressed thus, the king then asked him this again:
'Tell the arrangement of the sesame-cow; having made it accordingly, I shall give it.' / The family priest said: / 'Listen, O lord of men, to the ritual procedure for the sesame-cow.
The cow should consist of sixteen āḍhakas, and the calf should be made of four. / The legs are made of sugarcane stalks, and the teeth are auspicious flowers;
her nose is made of perfumes, and likewise her tongue of jaggery. / A garland should be fashioned for her tail, adorned with bells and ornaments.
Having fashioned such a one, one should fashion her with golden horns, / with silver hooves, and a bronze milking vessel, according to the rule for cows of old.
Having made it, O king, one should quickly give it to a brāhmaṇa with mantras— / the auspicious cow placed on a black antelope skin, covered with garments,
bound with a cord, accompanied by the five jewels, / supplied with all medicinal herbs, and purified with mantras, one should give it:
“May food and drink and all juices immediately arise for me; / fulfill our desires, O sesame-cow bestowed upon the twice-born!”
“O goddess, I receive you with devotion, especially for the sake of my family; / grant all desires, O sesame-cow, homage to you!”
The sesame-cow given in this manner, O best of kings, / brings about the attainment of all desires; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, a water-cow fashioned here with jars, / when given according to rule, immediately bestows all desires.
Likewise, a hundred cows given under the observance of the full moon day / become the grantors of all desires in heaven, just like Sāvitrī.
Likewise, a ghee-cow given according to rule by the wise / brings about the attainment of all desires and becomes the bestower of splendour.
Likewise, a juice-cow given in the month of Kārttika, O ruler of the earth, / grants all desires and always bestows a [lofty] destination.
All this has been explained to you in brief, though very extensive; / boundless fruit has been designated by Brahmā for every rite.
Since you are afflicted by thirst and hunger, O best of kings, / that gift is to be given in Kārttika; give it first, O lord of men.
A cosmic egg, complete with everything, endowed with creatures, jewels, and herbs, / and accompanied by gods, Dānavas, and Yakṣas, O lord,
having fashioned this entirely and furnished it on all sides with silver, / enriched with fine jewels, sun, and moon, on the twelfth day in Kārttika,
or on the fifteenth day of Kārttika, and at no other time, / a devoted man should give it to his family priest and guru.
Whatever beings abide within the womb of the cosmic egg, O ruler of the earth, / they are truly given by him; this has been told to you in brief.
Whatever fruit [belongs] to one who sacrifices with sacrifices completed with excellent priestly gifts, O king, / all that fruit especially belongs to [giving] a part of the cosmic egg.'
Moreover, whatever man bestows this entire Brahmā-egg, / by him recitation has been done, oblation offered, study performed, and praise sung.
The king said: / By performing the rite of giving the Brahmā-egg, one would become a sharer in liberation. / Tell me all—the time, place, priest, and holy place, O sinless one,
