by performing which I may become a partaker of the fruit of everything, / and from this contemptible existence liberation may swiftly come to me.
Vasiṣṭha said: / Hearing this, O king, his noble twice-born chaplain / had a golden Brahmā-egg fashioned out of all minerals.
Combined with a thousand niṣkas [of gold], he fashioned a lotus there; / and in its center stood Brahmā, adorned with rubies,
together with Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, with the ṛṣis and the sages, / all his sons beginning with Nārada, and the heaven-dwellers headed by Indra.
All were golden figures placed before Brahmā, / as well as the eternal Lord in the form of a boar, along with Lakṣmī.
One should use sapphire and emerald for his ornamentation, / and the wise man should produce his splendor with hessonite stones,
and the splendor of the moon with pearls, of the sun with diamonds; / and one should also assign golden figures for all the planets.
Silver should be seven times the gold, and copper should be seven times the silver; / brass must then be made seven times that, and bronze likewise seven times;
tin should be seven times the bronze, O king, / lead seven times the tin, and iron should be seven times the lead.
The seven continents and oceans, and the seven boundary mountains— / having made them to that measure by skilled craftsmen,
one should make the beings, trees, and so on, out of silver, / and one should fashion the wild creatures out of gold.
Trees, forest lords, shrubs, grasses, leaves, and creepers— / having prepared everything according to rule, it should be given at a sacred site by the wise.
At Kurukṣetra, at Gayā, at Prayāga, at Amarakankaṭa, / at Dvāravatī, at Prabhāsa, at Gaṅgādvāra, and at Puṣkara—
at these sacred sites it should be given, during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, / on all vulnerable days, and during the southern and northern solstices.
During a vyatīpāta it yields manifold fruit, and especially at the equinox; / this must be given, O best of kings; one should not hesitate at all.
Having engaged a householder maintaining the śālā fire, handsome and endowed with virtues, / and having honored him along with his wife and adorned him with ornaments,
making the family priest foremost, and other brāhmaṇas likewise, / endowed with the twenty-four qualities, were invited along with their wives.
He should present rings and ear-ornaments as well; / having thus honored them, standing well-composed before them,
bowing down again and again with prostrations of the eight limbs, / and folding his hands before the priest, [he said]:
"May you brāhmaṇas be pleased and favor me with friendship; / through your graciousness, O best of brāhmaṇas, I am made all the more pure.
Through the bond of your pleasure, the Grandfather himself is pleased; / and by this gift of the cosmic egg, may Janārdana attain satisfaction.
May the Lord Pinākapāṇi and Śakra, ruler of the thirty gods, / attain satisfaction through your meditation, O best of brāhmaṇas."
Having praised thus the brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas, the king / then gave the cosmic egg to the teacher in proper fashion, in that very moment.
Satisfied with all desires, the king then went to heaven; / and that gift was divided by that teacher together with the brāhmaṇas.
It was given by him to the others also, along with the cosmic egg, O king. / In the gift of a cosmic egg and in the gift of land, there should not be only a single recipient.
If he accepts it alone, he incurs guilt, the murder of a brāhmaṇa, no doubt. / It should be given in the presence of all, proclaiming it aloud.
And those who look upon it while it is being given are also purified; / through the very sight of it they are liberated, no doubt.
That which is called Bhīmadvādaśī: gold, water, and an antelope skin— / having prepared these, let them look upon them; by the sight of these, the fruit of the rite
is obtained effortlessly, as well as residence in the same world as the performer. / Cows are always to be bowed to with this mantra, O ruler of earth:
"Homage to the cows, the auspicious daughters of Surabhi; / homage to the pure daughters of Brahmā; homage, homage!"
And by remembering this mantra, one obtains the fruit of giving a cow. / Therefore, O king of kings, at the supreme sacred site Puṣkara,
especially on the full moon of Kārttika, you will attain the fruit of giving a cow. / Whatever sin exists, whether of a woman or of a man,
perishes completely by a mere bath at Puṣkara. / Whatever sacred sites there are on earth as far as the ocean, O Bhārata,
they all approach Puṣkara, especially on the full moon of Kārttika.

1.35.m: Bhīṣma said: / Everything has been spoken by your lordship along with the foundation in the Purāṇas, / and also how the cosmic egg was bestowed by Śveta upon his teacher.
Having heard this, a curiosity arose [as to] how licking a bone was done by him / for the sake of dispelling hunger, for lack of the gift of food, O brāhmaṇa.
That I wish to hear: which kings on earth / have attained heaven through the gift of food, and which sacrifices are rooted in food.
How was the intellect of that great-souled Śveta lost, / so that no gift of food was given by him, nor shown to him by the ṛṣis?
Ah, the glory of food, the fruit of which when given here / is enjoyed by men in the next world, and heaven becomes imperishable!
The brāhmaṇas, always rising up, extol the gift of food as supreme; / by the gift of food, the three worlds are enjoyed here by the lord of the gods.
He is called Śatakratu by all the best of brāhmaṇas; / by that he, the ruler of the thirty gods, attained an equal station.
Through giving alone he went to heaven; everything has been heard by me from you. / And if any other ancient event occurred at any time,
I wish to hear it further; tell that to me, O high-minded one. / Pulastya said: / This narrative was formerly told by the great-souled Agastya
to Rāma, O king; that I shall narrate to you now. / Bhīṣma said: / In what lineage was that Rāma born, that best of kings,
to whom this ancient legendary history was narrated by Agastya? / Pulastya said: / In the lineage of Raghu was born the one named Rāma, of great might;
the purpose of the gods was accomplished by him, and Rāvaṇa was slain in Laṅkā. / When he was established on the throne of the earth, ṛṣis came to his house.
Those great-souled ones arrived at the residence of Rāghava. / Then the doorkeeper, by the word of Agastya, quickly
announced the arrived ṛṣis, and full of haste, / seeing Rāma like the full moon risen, the gatekeeper [said]:
"O son of Kausalyā, may prosperity be yours! Good dawn to you after this night! / To behold your prosperity today, O delight of Raghu,
Agastya, along with the sages, stands at the gate, O king." / Having heard of the arrived sages, who were radiant like the sun, Rāma
then said to the doorkeeper: "Bring them in with haste! / For what reason were the best of sages held back by you at the door?"
At Rāma's command, he ushered in those sages comfortably; / and seeing those sages who had arrived, with joined palms in greeting,
Rāma greeted them, bowed, and seated them on seats. / And they, those bulls among sages, sat down all around on comfortable seats,
adorned with gold, spread with good rugs, and overlaid with kuśa grass. / The family priest offered water for washing the feet, sipping water, and respectful offerings.
Inquired after their welfare by Rāma, all those ṛṣis, / the great ṛṣis who knew the Vedas, spoke this word:
"Welfare to you, O mighty-armed delight of Raghu, everywhere! / By good fortune we see you prosperous, with your enemies slain!"

“Your wife Sītā was abducted by that wicked, most evil Rāvaṇa;
O tiger of the Raghu lineage, he was slain solely through her power.

And single-handed, without any ally, he was killed by you in battle, O Rāma!
No one exists who could perform such a deed as you have performed.

We came here to converse [with you], and having seen [you], we are now purified;
O king of kings, all the ascetics have become [blessed] by seeing you.

Today, tears have been wiped away by you through the slaying of Rāvaṇa,
having granted to the world, O hero, this auspicious gift of freedom from fear.

Hail to you, O descendant of Kakutstha of unmeasured valor, growing in victory!
You have been seen and spoken to; we shall now depart to our own hermitages.

When you entered the forest, Indra's bow was presented by me,
as well as two inexhaustible quivers and armor, O scorcher of foes.

You must come once again to my hermitage, O bearer of the Raghu line!”
Having spoken thus, all those sages vanished.

When the foremost sages had departed, Rāma, best among upholders of dharma,
reflected: “What could that task be, spoken of by the sage?

‘You must come once again to my hermitage, O delight of the Raghus’—
I must certainly go to the presence of Agastya.

A secret of the gods is to be heard, and whatever other task he may speak of.”
While Rāma of immeasurable splendor was pondering thus, [he resolved:]

“I shall constantly perform dharma, for dharma is the supreme goal.”
He ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.

As he gave gifts and offered oblations, they passed like a single year
for the great-souled Rāghava as he protected his subjects.

On that very day, an elderly brāhmaṇa from the countryside
came to Rāma's door, carrying his dead son.

He uttered various words filled with expressions of affection:
“What evil deed, O son, was committed by me in a previous life,

that I behold you, an only son, gone to death—
a boy who had not reached youth, five years old, his life departed,

overcome by death untimely, to my sorrow, O my little son,
gone to the realm of Yama without having performed the ancestral rites?

Clearly it is an evil deed of Rāma by which death has come to you!
The murder of a child, the murder of a brāhmaṇa, and the murder of a woman

will undoubtedly enter into Rāghava when I and my wife have died!”
Rāghava heard everything, filled with sorrow and grief.

Restraining that brāhmaṇa, Rāma addressed Vasiṣṭha with these words:
“What should be done by me today when such a matter has arisen?

Shall I sacrifice my life in fire, or shall I throw myself from a mountain?
How can I attain purification after hearing what the brāhmaṇa has spoken?”

Standing before Vasiṣṭha and the wretched king, Nārada
then replied, having heard the words, in the presence of the ṛṣis:

“Listen, O Rāma, how in the course of time the demise of the child has occurred.
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, O Rāma, the brāhmaṇa was supreme everywhere.

No non-brāhmaṇa performed austerities, O Rāghava;
then all were free from untimely death, born long-lived.

When the Tretā age arrived next, the brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas were supreme;
in the Dvāpara age, their adharma entered the vaiśyas and the śūdras.

Thus practiced continuously, falsehood arose again;
three quarters of adharma and one of dharma had arrived.

Then the earlier castes, beginning with the brāhmaṇas, were deeply alarmed;
yet the second quarter of dharma came into being.

In that age called Dvāpara, austerity entered the vaiśya;
the lack of dharma of the three ages stood against dharma.

When that age called Kali arrived, being the final cosmic age,
adharma and falsehood both increased, O bull among men.

The practice of austerity in the śūdra womb will occur in the Kali age;
he is on the border of your realm, O king, performing fiercer austerity.

An evil-minded śūdra performs austerity; by that, the death of the boy has been caused.
For in whose realm, O king,

or in whose city, O tiger among kings, an evil-minded man commits adharma or an unlawful act,
he quickly goes to hell until the dissolution of all beings,

and the ruler of the earth incurs a fourth part of that sin.
Therefore, O tiger among men, go to your realm.

Wherever you see an evil deed, take action there.
In this way, the increase of your dharma and the increase of your army

shall come to pass, O best of men, as well as the revival of this child.”
Addressed thus by Nārada, the delight of the Raghus was filled with wonder,

attained incomparable joy, and said this to Lakṣmaṇa:
“Go, gentle one, Lakṣmaṇa, console the best of brāhmaṇas,

and place the body of the boy in a trough of oil
with the most excellent perfumes and fragrant oils,

so that the boy does not decay; act thus, gentle one,
so that the body of the child of unblemished deeds may be preserved.

Act in such a way that no ruin or decomposition occurs.”
Having thus instructed Saumitri, Lakṣmaṇa of auspicious marks,

he of great renown mentally meditated on Puṣpaka: “Come!”
Understanding that gesture, the wish-moving aerial chariot adorned with gold

came within moments into the presence of Rāghava.
With folded hands it spoke these words: “Here I am, O king of men,

standing before you, O mighty-armed one, as your servant.”
Having heard the speech of Puṣpaka for some time, O king,

he saluted those great ṛṣis and mounted the aerial chariot,
having taken his bow, two quivers, and a sword of great luster.

Leaving both heroes, Saumitri and Bharata, in the city,
he set forth quickly toward the west, searching with focused mind.

Afterward he went to the northern direction bordering the Himavat;
and going to the eastern direction also, observing in the same manner, the ruler of men

found all of pure conduct, spotless like a mirror.
Then the delight of the Raghus traversed the southern direction.

On the northern side of a mountain, he saw a very large lake;
at that lake, performing severe austerity, an ascetic

Rāghava saw: terrible, hanging upside down.
Approaching that ascetic engaged in penance, the descendant of Kakutstha,

Rāghava, spoke these words: “Blessed are you, shining like an immortal!
In what caste do you have your origin of growing austerity, O firm of resolve?

I, Rāma, son of Daśaratha, ask you out of curiosity:
what purpose have you resolved upon—heaven, or something else?

Or for what reason do you practice tapas? I wish to hear, O ascetic.
Are you a brāhmaṇa—blessings to you—or an invincible kṣatriya,

or a vaiśya of the third caste, or a śūdra? Let the truth be spoken!
Austerity is ever of the nature of truth in gaining the heavenly realm.

Austerity of the nature of truth is both sāttvika and rājasa;
for it was created by Brahmā indeed for the sake of helping the world.

That which is fierce, born of kṣatriya power, is said to be rājasa;
and that which is for the destruction of another is declared to be demonic.

Or he who conceals his limbs smeared with blood part by part,
or practices the five-fire penance for accomplishment or for death—

this disposition of yours is indeed demonic, and I do not consider you a twice-born.
Accomplishment belongs to you if you speak the truth; by falsehood there is no life.”
Hearing those words of Rāma, of unwearied action, / [the ascetic], being thus hanging upside down, spoke these words:
"Welcome to you, best of kings! After a long time you are seen, O Rāghava. / I have become your son, and you have become a father to me, O sinless one.
Or rather, it is not merely so: the king is indeed the father of all. / As such, you are to be honored, O king; we perform asceticism in your realm.
We perform it, and there is a share for you in it, ordained of old by the Self-born. / We are not blessed, O Rāma; you alone are blessed, O king,
in whose realm ascetics indeed seek attainment in this manner. / By my asceticism, O Rāghava, obtain attainment.
As for what you asked—'In what womb [were you born] and of what nature is your asceticism?'— / I was born from a Śūdra womb, and have undertaken fierce asceticism.
I pray for godhood with my own body, O Rāma of good vows! / I do not speak falsely, O king, out of a desire to conquer the realm of the gods.
Know me to be a Śūdra, O Kākutstha, Śambūka by name." / As he was speaking, Kākutstha, unsheathing from its scabbard
a bright, spotless sword, Rāghava severed his head. / When that Śūdra was slain, the gods, accompanied by Indra and led by Agni,
praised Kākutstha again and again, saying, "Well done! Well done!" / And a great, fragrant shower of flowers of the gods,
discharged from the sky, scattered all around Rāghava. / And highly pleased, the gods spoke to Rāma, the foremost of those who know speech:
"This deed for the gods has been accomplished by you, O gentle delight of the Raghus. / Accept a boon, O Rāma, whatever you desire, O one of great vows!
For because of you, this Śūdra has gone to heaven with his body." / Hearing the words of the gods, Rāghava, very composed,
spoke with joined palms to the thousand-eyed Purandara: / "If the gods are pleased with me, or if I am worthy of a boon,
and if they are pleased with my deed, let that son of the Brahmin live! / Indeed, this is the boon desired by me from you, my supreme wish.
Through my fault that young boy, the only son of the Brahmin, / before his time had arrived, was carried off by Time to the abode of Vivasvat's son.
Bring him to life, may you be blessed, so that I may not become a liar to the elder! / For the matter was promised to the Brahmin: 'I shall revive your son.'
Let the child live through a quarter or a half of my own lifespan, O gods! / This boon, chosen by me, is superior to ten million boons."
Hearing that speech of Rāghava, the best of the gods, / delighted and filled with affection, replied to the great-souled one:
"Be at ease, O Kākutstha! The only son of the Brahmin / has regained life once more, and is reunited with his kinsmen.
At the very moment, O Kākutstha, that this Śūdra was struck down, / at that very moment he was suddenly joined with life.
Attain well-being! Good fortune to you; we are departing, O scorcher of foes! / We are going to the hermitage of Agastya to see the great sage."
Saying "So be it" in assent to the gods, the delight of the Raghus / mounted that Puṣpaka celestial chariot adorned with gold.
